claim: JCVI-syn3A has a 543 kbp genome and 493 genes.
source: JCVI-syn3A, a robust minimal cell with a 543 kbp genome and 493 genes, provides a versatile platform to study the basics of life.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as a basic characteristic of JCVI-syn3A

claim: The metabolic network model for JCVI-syn3A has 98% of enzymatic reactions supported by annotation or experiment.
source: Using the vast amount of experimental information available on its precursor, Mycoplasma mycoides capri, we assembled a near-complete metabolic network with 98% of enzymatic reactions supported by annotation or experiment.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a result of the reconstruction process

claim: The model shows a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.59 when compared to genome-scale in vivo transposon mutagenesis experiments.
source: The model agrees well with genome-scale in vivo transposon mutagenesis experiments, showing a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.59.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a measure of agreement between model and experiment

claim: 92% of genes in the reconstruction have high in vivo essentiality or quasi-essentiality (68% essential).
source: The genes in the reconstruction have a high in vivo essentiality or quasi-essentiality of 92% (68% essential), compared to 79% in silico essentiality.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a result of transposon mutagenesis analysis

claim: The model identifies 30 essential genes with unclear function.
source: Finally, the identification of 30 essential genes with unclear function will motivate the search for new biological mechanisms beyond metabolism.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a finding from the model

claim: Mycoplasmas have small genomes (580–1350 kbp) lacking a cell wall.
source: It has long been suggested (Morowitz, 1984) that a model to study the basics of cellular life would be the mycoplasmas—a group of bacteria with small genomes (580–1350 kbp (Herrmann, 1992; Fraser et al., 1995)) lacking a cell wall, which evolved via extreme genome reduction from low GC content Gram-positive ancestors (Pollack et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Herrmann, 1992; Fraser et al., 1995; and Pollack et al., 1997

claim: Mycoplasma genitalium has a 580 kbp genome with 525 genes overall (482 for proteins, 43 for RNAs).
source: The genome of the human urogenital pathogen Mycoplasma genitalium (580 kbp, 525 genes overall, 482 for proteins, 43 for RNAs), sequenced in 1995 (Fraser et al., 1995), is the smallest genome of any autonomously replicating cell found in nature and has thus been deemed a close approximation to a minimal genome (Glass et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fraser et al., 1995 and Glass et al., 2006

claim: Transposon mutagenesis studies suggested 382 out of 482 protein-coding genes in M. genitalium to be essential.
source: In M. genitalium, such studies have suggested 382 out of the 482 protein-coding genes to be essential (Glass et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Glass et al., 2006

claim: JCVI-syn3.0 has a 531 kbp genome containing 473 genes (438 protein-coding genes and 35 genes for RNAs).
source: Starting with the gene sequence from the 1079 kbp genome of the ruminant pathogen Mycoplasma mycoides capri serovar LC GM12, a minimal genome of 531 kbp was designed and constructed containing 473 genes (438 protein-coding genes and 35 genes for RNAs) (Hutchison et al., 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hutchison et al., 2016a

claim: JCVI-syn3.0 has a genome smaller than that of any independently-replicating cell found in nature.
source: The resulting strain, JCVI-syn3.0 (NCBI GenBank: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/CP014940.1 (Hutchison et al., 2016b)), has a genome smaller than that of any independently-replicating cell found in nature and is considered to be our 'working approximation to a minimal cell'.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hutchison et al., 2016b

claim: JCVI-syn3.0 had a doubling time of 2–3 hr compared to 1 hr for JCVI-syn1.0.
source: Phenotypic traits of JCVI-syn3.0 included extensive filamentation and vesicle formation during growth, and a doubling time of 2–3 hr (compared to the spheroidal morphology and 1 hr doubling time conferred by the JCVI-syn1.0 genome).
evidence: Stated as an observed phenotypic trait

claim: JCVI-syn3A has a doubling time of approximately 2 hr.
source: JCVI-syn3A has a doubling time of ∼2 hr and consistently forms spherical cells of approximately 400 nm in diameter.
evidence: Stated as an observed characteristic of JCVI-syn3A

claim: JCVI-syn3A consistently forms spherical cells of approximately 400 nm in diameter.
source: JCVI-syn3A has a doubling time of ∼2 hr and consistently forms spherical cells of approximately 400 nm in diameter.
evidence: Stated as an observed characteristic of JCVI-syn3A

claim: JCVI-syn3A has 452 protein-coding genes and 38 RNA genes.
source: With a 543 kbp genome containing 493 genes of which 452 code for proteins and 38 for RNAs, JCVI-syn3A still has a smaller genome than any natural autonomously replicating cell while providing a robust and versatile platform to study the basics of life.
evidence: Stated as a characteristic of JCVI-syn3A

claim: JCVI-syn3A has the smallest ratio of genes involved in metabolism to those in genetic information processing among JCVI-syn3A, M. pneumoniae, and E. coli.
source: Among the model bacteria E. coli and the related and well-studied (Güell et al., 2009; Kühner et al., 2009; Yus et al., 2009; Maier et al., 2011; Wodke et al., 2013) Mycoplasma pneumoniae, JCVI-syn3A has the smallest ratio of genes involved in metabolism to those in genetic information processing.
evidence: Stated as a comparison between organisms, with citations supporting the characterization of M. pneumoniae

claim: JCVI-syn3A has 91 genes with no known (unclear) function compared to 311 for M. pneumoniae and 1780 for E. coli.
source: With 91 it also has the smallest number of genes that are considered to have no known (unclear) function compared to 311 and 1780 for M. pneumoniae and E. coli, respectively (see Table 1 and Supplementary file 1C–1D for an itemized account of the functional categories for the three genomes).
evidence: Stated as a comparison between organisms

claim: The metabolic reconstruction for JCVI-syn3A features 338 reactions organized in nine subsystems.
source: Our model features 338 reactions organized in nine subsystems (see Supplementary file 1B), involving 304 metabolites, catalyzed by gene products of 155 genes, thus covering a third of the genes of JCVI-syn3A.
evidence: Stated as a description of the model

claim: The metabolic reconstruction involves 304 metabolites.
source: Our model features 338 reactions organized in nine subsystems (see Supplementary file 1B), involving 304 metabolites, catalyzed by gene products of 155 genes, thus covering a third of the genes of JCVI-syn3A.
evidence: Stated as a description of the model

claim: The metabolic reconstruction is catalyzed by gene products of 155 genes.
source: Our model features 338 reactions organized in nine subsystems (see Supplementary file 1B), involving 304 metabolites, catalyzed by gene products of 155 genes, thus covering a third of the genes of JCVI-syn3A.
evidence: Stated as a description of the model

claim: The metabolic reconstruction covers a third of the genes of JCVI-syn3A.
source: Our model features 338 reactions organized in nine subsystems (see Supplementary file 1B), involving 304 metabolites, catalyzed by gene products of 155 genes, thus covering a third of the genes of JCVI-syn3A.
evidence: Stated as a description of the model

claim: Of the 452 coding genes in JCVI-syn3A, 60% are essential, 25% are quasi-essential, and 15% are non-essential by transposon mutagenesis analysis.
source: Of the 452 coding genes in JCVI-syn3A, 60% are essential, 25% are quasi-essential, and 15% are non-essential by this analysis.
evidence: Stated as a result of transposon mutagenesis analysis

claim: Of the 91 genes of unclear function in JCVI-syn3A, 30 are essential, 32 are quasi-essential, and 29 are non-essential.
source: The detailed breakdown of the JCVI-syn3A genome into these classes (Table 1) shows that of the 91 genes of unclear function, 30 are essential, 32 are quasi-essential, and 29 are non-essential.
evidence: Stated as a result of transposon mutagenesis analysis

claim: The 30 essential genes of unclear function could represent new biological mechanisms not yet defined.
source: Those 30 essential genes could represent new biological mechanisms not yet defined and should motivate the search to discover their function (Alberts, 2011).
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the findings, with citation to Alberts, 2011

claim: 123 of the 155 genes included in the model are essential (79%) by in silico analysis.
source: By this definition, 123 of the 155 genes included in the model are essential (79%).
evidence: Stated as a result of in silico gene knockout analysis

claim: All in silico essential genes are at least quasi-essential in vivo.
source: We find that transposon- and model-derived gene essentiality agree well, with every in silico essential gene being at least quasi-essential in vivo (i.e. removal might not be immediately detrimental, but give a growth disadvantage).
evidence: Stated as a result of comparing in silico and in vivo essentiality

claim: JCVI-syn3A spends only ~6% of ATP on (small molecule) metabolic processes.
source: In line with JCVI-syn3A relying heavily on uptake of pre-formed precursors and further conversion through salvage pathways only, it spends only ∼6% of ATP on (small molecule) metabolic processes (i.e. lipids, cofactors and nucleotides, plus PRPP synthesis in the pentose phosphate pathway).
evidence: Stated as a result of energy usage analysis

claim: The vast majority of energy (75%) in JCVI-syn3A is spent directly on growth.
source: The vast majority of energy (75%) is spent directly on growth, that is macromolecular synthesis and tRNA charging and the non-quantifiable contribution to GAM.
evidence: Stated as a result of energy usage analysis

claim: A modest fraction of ~16% of cellular energy expenses in JCVI-syn3A falls to the NGAM (macromolecular turnover and ATPase).
source: A modest fraction of ∼16% of cellular energy expenses falls to the NGAM (macromolecular turnover and ATPase).
evidence: Stated as a result of energy usage analysis

claim: In M. pneumoniae, non-growth associated maintenance accounts for 71–88% of total cellular ATP consumption.
source: These numbers stand in striking difference to M. pneumoniae, for which non-growth associated maintenance accounts for 71–88% of total cellular ATP consumption (in the accounting for M. pneumoniae, the NGAM does not include protein/RNA turnover) (Wodke et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wodke et al., 2013

claim: M. pneumoniae has a doubling time between 8 and 20 hr.
source: This correlates with M. pneumoniae having a doubling time between 8 and 20 hr (Yus et al., 2009; Wodke et al., 2013), that is four to ten times slower than JCVI-syn3A.
evidence: Supported by citations to Yus et al., 2009 and Wodke et al., 2013

claim: Transport processes account for ~3% of ATP consumption in JCVI-syn3A.
source: The ATP breakdown also reveals that in spite of the minimal cell's heavy reliance on uptake of pre-formed precursors, transport processes only account for ∼3% of ATP consumption.
evidence: Stated as a result of energy usage analysis

claim: The only annotated sugar importer in the JCVI-syn3A genome is the glucose PTS system comprising PtsI, PtsH, Crr and PtsG.
source: The only annotated sugar importer in the JCVI-syn3A genome is the glucose PTS system comprising PtsI (ptsI/0233), PtsH (ptsH/0694), Crr (glucose-specific IIA component, crr/0234) and PtsG (ptsG/0779).
evidence: Stated as a result of annotation analysis

claim: Secretion of acetate, lactate and pyruvate has been observed in M. mycoides.
source: Secretion of acetate (Rodwell and Rodwell, 1954), lactate (Rodwell, 1967) and pyruvate (Rodwell, 1969) has been observed in M. mycoides; with mutational data on M. mycoides mycoides T1 (Lee et al., 1986) indicating a common transporter for pyruvate and lactate.
evidence: Supported by citations to Rodwell and Rodwell, 1954; Rodwell, 1967; Rodwell, 1969; and Lee et al., 1986

claim: The JCVI-syn3A annotation contains a putative ribonucleoside (RNS) ABC import system.
source: The JCVI-syn3A annotation contains a putative ribonucleoside (RNS) ABC import system (rnsD/0008 through rnsB/0011), which is assumed to import all nucleosides (ribo- and deoxyribo-), but no individual bases or free ribose, in accordance with the experimental characterization of the ribonucleoside ABC importer in Streptococcus mutans (Webb and Hosie, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Webb and Hosie, 2006

claim: M. mycoides capri LC Y was found to be unable to utilize folate itself.
source: Furthermore, M. mycoides capri LC Y was found to be unable to utilize folate itself (Neale et al., 1981), in line with JCVI-syn3A lacking a gene coding for dihydrofolate reductase.
evidence: Supported by citation to Neale et al., 1981

claim: The genome of JCVI-syn3A contains pathways for NAD(P) and FMN/FAD formation from nicotinate and riboflavin.
source: For downstream conversion, the genome contains pathways for NAD(P) and FMN/FAD formation from nicotinate and riboflavin.
evidence: Stated as a result of annotation analysis

claim: JCVI-syn3A shares the fatty acid utilization pathway from Staphylococcus aureus.
source: JCVI-syn3A shares the fatty acid utilization pathway from Staphylococcus aureus (Parsons et al., 2014), which starts with phosphorylation of free fatty acids in the membrane and subsequent binding to glycerol phosphate (by plsY/0117) and acyl carrier protein (ACP, by plsX/0419).
evidence: Supported by citation to Parsons et al., 2014

claim: The genome of JCVI-syn3A contains a putative oligopeptide ABC importer (Opp/Ami, oppB/0165 through oppA/0169).
source: The genome of JCVI-syn3A contains a putative oligopeptide ABC importer (Opp/Ami, oppB/0165 through oppA/0169).
evidence: Stated as a result of annotation analysis

claim: In Lactococcus lactis, the Opp system has been found to import peptides of four to at least 35 amino acids with little dependence of uptake rates on peptide length or amino acid composition.
source: In Lactococcus lactis, the Opp system has been found to import peptides of four to at least 35 amino acids with little dependence of uptake rates on peptide length or amino acid composition (Detmers et al., 1998; Doeven et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Detmers et al., 1998 and Doeven et al., 2004

claim: M. mycoides capri LC Y has been found capable of taking up all amino acids in their free form.
source: However, M. mycoides capri LC Y has been found capable of taking up all amino acids in their free form (Rodwell, 1969) (glutamic and aspartic acid not investigated); thus, the least constraining assumption is made that both permeases can take up all amino acids, except for glutamic and aspartic acid, whose uptake is already enabled by GltP.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rodwell, 1969

claim: The JCVI-syn3A annotation lists importers for magnesium (mgtA/0787) and phosphate (Pst system, pstS/0425 through pstB/0427).
source: The JCVI-syn3A annotation lists importers for magnesium (mgtA/0787) and phosphate (Pst system, pstS/0425 through pstB/0427); Danchin and Fang (2016) have suggested the putative magnesium import gene corA/0879 could import calcium as well based on its similarity to the B. subtilis calcium importer YloB (Raeymaekers et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Danchin and Fang, 2016 and Raeymaekers et al., 2002

claim: The model for JCVI-syn3A has a total GAM of 46.54 mmol gDW−1.
source: Together with the ATP costs for macromolecular synthesis, this yields a total GAM of 46.54 mmol gDW−1, which is comparable to the 53.95 mmol gDW−1 estimated for E. coli (Orth et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated as a result of model construction, with citation to Orth et al., 2011 for comparison

claim: The total NGAM in the model for JCVI-syn3A is 3.30 mmol gDW−1 h−1.
source: The resulting total NGAM in the model for JCVI-syn3A is then 3.30 mmol gDW−1 h-1, which comes out similar to the iJO1366 model for E. coli (3.15 mmol gDW−1 h-1) (Orth et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated as a result of model construction, with citation to Orth et al., 2011 for comparison

claim: The purine incorporation flux into RNA in M. mycoides capri LC Y has been determined as 0.5–1.0 nmol/min/mg cellular protein, corresponding to 0.016–0.033 mmol gDW−1 h−1.
source: The purine incorporation flux into RNA has been determined for M. mycoides capri LC Y (Mitchell et al., 1978) as 0.5–1.0 nmol/min/mg cellular protein, corresponding to 0.016–0.033 mmol gDW−1 h-1.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mitchell et al., 1978

claim: The in silico net flux of ATP and GTP into RNA is 0.047 and 0.043 mmol gDW−1 h−1, respectively.
source: This is close to the in silico net flux of ATP and GTP into RNA of 0.047 and 0.043 mmol gDW−1 h-1, respectively.
evidence: Stated as a result of the FBA model

claim: The in silico K+ uptake is 0.29 mmol gDW−1 h−1.
source: The in silico K+ uptake of 0.29 mmol gDW−1 h-1 also falls within a factor of two of the experimental uptake rate of 0.49 mmol gDW−1 h-1 (15 nmol/min/mg cellular protein) in M. mycoides capri PG3 (Benyoucef et al., 1982a).
evidence: Stated as a result of the FBA model, with citation to Benyoucef et al., 1982a for comparison

claim: M. mycoides capri LC Y spends 10% of its glucose uptake on polysaccharide capsule production.
source: Furthermore, it has been reported that M. mycoides capri LC Y spends 10% of its glucose uptake on polysaccharide capsule production (Plackett, 1967a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Plackett, 1967a

claim: The in silico flux through phosphoglucomutase is 0.135 mmol gDW−1 h−1, amounting to 1.8% of glucose uptake.
source: As can be seen, the in silico flux through phosphoglucomutase (PGMT, deoB/0733, leading from glucose-6-phosphate to galactan and Gal-DAG in Figures 6 and 10) is lower than the experimental value, amounting to only 1.8% (0.135 mmol gDW−1 h-1, from 7.4 mmol gDW−1 h-1 glucose taken up).
evidence: Stated as a result of the FBA model

claim: The model reproduces the splitting between galactan and Gal-DAG production with a ratio of ~22:1.
source: However, the model does qualitatively reproduce the further splitting between galactan and Gal-DAG production, which gives a ratio of ∼22:1 (UDP-galactofuranose consumption of 0.129 mmol gDW−1 h-1 vs. 0.006 mmol gDW−1 h-1), compared to a ratio of ∼64:1 from 3H labeling (Plackett, 1967a).
evidence: Stated as a result of the FBA model, with citation to Plackett, 1967a for comparison

claim: The model for JCVI-syn3A has 338 reactions involving 304 metabolites, catalyzed by gene products of 155 genes.
source: The metabolic reconstruction of JCVI-syn3A features 338 reactions involving 304 metabolites, catalyzed by gene products of 155 genes, thus covering a third of the genome.
evidence: Stated as a description of the model

claim: The model for M. pneumoniae (iJW145) includes 304 reactions involving the products of 145 genes.
source: With a published metabolic reconstruction (iJW145 (Wodke et al., 2013)) that includes 304 reactions involving the products of 145 genes it is similar in size to the metabolic reconstruction of the minimal cell JCVI-syn3A with its 338 reactions and 155 genes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wodke et al., 2013

claim: The JCVI-syn3A model has 6% gap fills out of all model reactions, compared to 25% in the M. pneumoniae model iJW145.
source: Utilizing the vast experimental information on M. mycoides capri, the natural precursor of JCVI-syn3A, as well as information on JCVI-syn3A homologs in other organisms, enabled us to obtain a smaller percentage of gap fills (i.e. model reactions assumed to be enzymatic yet having no gene assigned) of 6% out of all model reactions, compared to 25% in the M. pneumoniae model iJW145; or 9% for JCVI-syn3A vs. 32%, if exchange, macromolecular and biomass reactions are excluded from the total number of reactions in each model.
evidence: Stated as a comparison between models

claim: The JCVI-syn3A model yields a higher degree of in silico essentiality (79%) compared to 56% for the 131 'metabolic proteins' in the M. pneumoniae model.
source: The JCVI-syn3A model yields a higher degree of in silico essentiality (79% vs. 56% for the 131 'metabolic proteins' in the M. pneumoniae model (Wodke et al., 2013))—reflecting the minimization of the JCVI-syn3A genome.
evidence: Stated as a comparison between models, with citation to Wodke et al., 2013

claim: A core of 126 reactions is shared between the JCVI-syn3A and M. pneumoniae models.
source: Excluding exchange, macromolecular and biomass reactions, a core of 126 reactions is shared between the models, including glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway, reactions from nucleotide, cofactor and lipid salvage pathways, and tRNA charging.
evidence: Stated as a result of model comparison

claim: M. pneumoniae has 116 reactions not present in JCVI-syn3A.
source: However, M. pneumoniae has 116 reactions not present in JCVI-syn3A, which mainly includes uptake and utilization of additional sugar sources, further nucleotide conversions, more extensive cofactor salvage reactions, and additional lipid-related reactions.
evidence: Stated as a result of model comparison

claim: The JCVI-syn3A reconstruction contains 120 reactions not present in the M. pneumoniae model.
source: Interestingly, in spite of the much smaller genome of JCVI-syn3A, its reconstruction still contains 120 reactions not present in the M. pneumoniae model.
evidence: Stated as a result of model comparison

claim: JCVI-syn3A produces a polysaccharide capsule in addition to the monogalactosyl-lipid.
source: These include the production of a polysaccharide capsule (in addition to the monogalactosyl-lipid), some alternative sugar sources specific to JCVI-syn3A and also specific nucleotide conversion and breakdown reactions, perhaps most notably the presence of the essential damage preemption enzyme dUTPase (dut/0447, see Figure 8).
evidence: Stated as a difference between JCVI-syn3A and M. pneumoniae

claim: JCVI-syn3A contains the essential damage preemption enzyme dUTPase (dut/0447).
source: These include the production of a polysaccharide capsule (in addition to the monogalactosyl-lipid), some alternative sugar sources specific to JCVI-syn3A and also specific nucleotide conversion and breakdown reactions, perhaps most notably the presence of the essential damage preemption enzyme dUTPase (dut/0447, see Figure 8).
evidence: Stated as a difference between JCVI-syn3A and M. pneumoniae

claim: Neale et al. (1981) demonstrated the ability of M. mycoides capri to omit Met-tRNAfMet formylation and to initiate protein synthesis with the unformylated species in the absence of folate in the media without significant change in doubling time.
source: Intriguingly, however, Neale et al. (1981) demonstrated the ability of M. mycoides capri to omit Met-tRNAfMet formylation, and to initiate protein synthesis with the unformylated species, in the absence of folate in the media–without significant change in doubling time.
evidence: Supported by citation to Neale et al., 1981

claim: Translational mistakes introduced by enzyme knockouts can sum up and become detrimental once a certain threshold is crossed.
source: It is generally known that translational mistakes, such as those introduced by enzyme knockouts, can sum up and become detrimental once a certain threshold is crossed.
evidence: Stated as general knowledge

claim: Thiouridine tRNA modification through IscS and MnmA appears to be non-essential in M. mycoides capri LC Y.
source: In the genome of JCVI-syn3A, there already seems to be a precedent for this threshold scenario: Thiouridine tRNA modification through IscS and MnmA (iscS/0441 and mnmA/0387) appears to be non-essential in M. mycoides capri LC Y, which can grow without a precursor for the IscS cofactor pyridoxal phosphate (Rodwell, 1969).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rodwell, 1969

claim: The transposon mutagenesis data for JCVI-syn3A indicate both iscS/0441 and mnmA/0387 to be essential.
source: However, the transposon mutagenesis data for JCVI-syn3A indicate both genes to be essential, which must hence be due to the removal of other genes.
evidence: Stated as a result of transposon mutagenesis analysis

claim: RmsB catalyzes the methylation of 16S rRNA C967 using S-adenosylmethionine and plays a role in translation initiation in E. coli.
source: RmsB catalyzes the methylation of 16S rRNA C967 using S-adenosylmethionine and plays a role in translation initiation in E. coli—both in binding of tRNAfMet (Burakovsky et al., 2012) and in fidelity of initiation (Arora et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Burakovsky et al., 2012 and Arora et al., 2013

claim: All genes from the pentose phosphate pathway are essential in silico but only quasi-essential in vivo, except for prs/0831 (PRPPS), which is essential in vivo.
source: While all genes from the pentose phosphate pathway are essential in silico, they are only quasi-essential in vivo—except for the final gene, prs/0831 (PRPPS), which converts ribose 5-phosphate (R5P) to the pathway end product PRPP.
evidence: Stated as a comparison between in silico and in vivo essentiality

claim: There is an alternative route to R5P in JCVI-syn3A, bypassing the rest of the pentose phosphate pathway by providing pentose sugars from nucleoside breakdown through deoB/0733 (PGMT/PPM).
source: This is noteworthy because with deoB/0733 (PGMT/PPM), there is an alternative route to R5P, bypassing the rest of the pentose phosphate pathway by providing pentose sugars from nucleoside breakdown.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the model and essentiality data

claim: Proton-symport coupled secretion of bases released from nucleosides has been suggested for mycoplasmas.
source: It is unclear how biologically realistic this scenario is, but proton-symport coupled secretion of bases released from nucleosides has been suggested for mycoplasmas, and has even been proposed to contribute to the transmembrane proton gradient (Maniloff, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maniloff, 1992

claim: The 12 true negatives from the essentiality comparison (genes non-essential both in silico and in vivo) are strong candidates for attempts to remove more genes.
source: The 12 true negatives from the essentiality comparison (genes non-essential both in silico and in vivo) are strong candidates for attempts to remove more genes, and hence minimize the genome of JCVI-syn3A even further.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the essentiality comparison

claim: All the true negatives except folT/0822 can be removed simultaneously in silico.
source: Except for folT/0822 in the last two suggested experiments, all listed genes can be removed simultaneously in silico, as any interdependencies between them do not pertain to essential functions.
evidence: Stated as a result of in silico analysis

claim: The resulting in silico doubling time after removing all true negatives simultaneously is 3.2 hr.
source: The resulting in silico doubling time is 3.2 hr, that is the same doubling time observed by knocking out any single gene along the acetate branch.
evidence: Stated as a result of in silico analysis

claim: If JCVI-syn3A could be shown to grow without folate usage, a removal of 10 genes might be possible.
source: Thus, a removal of 10 genes might be possible if JCVI-syn3A could be shown to grow without folate usage, or be enabled to do so (e.g. by reintroducing translation-related gene(s) whose removal might have raised the importance of Met-tRNAfMet formylation; see Section 'The role of folate metabolism').
evidence: Stated as a hypothetical scenario based on the model and essentiality data

claim: The expression profiles for essential and non-essential proteins are qualitatively similar both to each other and to the expression profile of all proteins in JCVI-syn3A.
source: As can be seen, the expression profiles for essential and non-essential proteins are qualitatively similar both to each other and to the expression profile of all proteins in JCVI-syn3A.
evidence: Stated as a result of proteomics analysis

claim: The similarity in expression profiles suggests the presence of little regulation, if at all, that would discriminate gene products based on their essentiality.
source: While this does not yet allow for strong conclusions, it does suggest the presence of little regulation, if at all, that would discriminate gene products based on their essentiality.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the proteomics data

claim: The conclusion about little regulation would be in line with the small number of identified regulatory proteins left in the genome of JCVI-syn3A.
source: This conclusion would be in line with the small number of identified regulatory proteins left in the genome of JCVI-syn3A.
evidence: Stated as supporting evidence for the interpretation
